Religiosity in Iran: The Need for a Theology of Coexistence and Solidarity

Are the gods dead? Has the secularization of societies in the modern era really eliminated religions? In this episode, Jabar Rahmani, a professor of the anthropology of religion, argues that contrary to popular belief, Iranians still lead religious lives; and religions, in their various manifestations, give meaning and direction to social life—even if they are not Abrahamic religions.

Watch the conversation
https://youtu.be/eC5X6W2hP0Y

According to Jabar Rahmani, although surveys show that the formal forms of religiosity have weakened over recent decades, informal forms of religiosity remain prominent in society and manifest through collective rituals.

He speaks of the need for religious forms grounded in solidarity and coexistence in order to preserve the integrity and peaceful living of Iranian life.

entry.title: [fazelimohammadir] Gentlemen in charge! A society squeezed economically by war, sanctions, and…
entry.summary:
Machine-translated from the original Telegram post.

Source: @fazelimohammadir

Gentlemen in charge! A society squeezed economically by war, sanctions, and siege becomes more sensitive, more on edge, and more vulnerable. The smallest social friction in such an environment carries a far higher cost than under normal conditions. A family grappling with inflation, job insecurity, anxiety over medicine, housing, and their children's future has far less capacity to absorb new tensions. At this point, the quality of social policy is directly linked to the country's ability to navigate the crisis. Every policy must be measured by a simple question: Does this policy, at this moment, strengthen social bonds or further inflame existing fractures? Provocative identity debates, cultural disputes such as hijab, the proposal to lash a female singer, the widespread criminalization of social behavior, measures that pit parts of society against other parts, and the reopening of cases like women's dress code are not merely cultural or legal matters. Under crisis conditions, these policies carry a secondary consequence as well: they divert part of society's political, disciplinary, and psychological energy away from the main problem and activate divisions that — you must accept — Iranian society has moved past and the people deserve respect for, yet under economic pressure these divisions have the potential to turn into social fractures. In this sense, a country in crisis needs something akin to a "social ceasefire" — meaning preventing the creation of conflicts that are not urgent and that can drain the country's limited social capital.

Security from Beyond Borders: The Necessity of the Axis of Resistance for Iran

Hadi Masoumi-Zare, a researcher of Middle Eastern studies, is a guest on IranTalk in this episode to discuss Iran's regional presence and the Axis of Resistance. Masoumi-Zare traces the genealogy of Iran's regional presence back to the Median period and shows that regional ties were one of the main factors that historically preserved the security of the Iranian homeland. Watch the conversation: https://youtu.be/1Bk_7Tcq0rY

He also believes that in recent centuries, due to Iran's cultural, religious, and linguistic distinctiveness compared to neighboring countries, Iran has suffered from a kind of strategic loneliness that doubles the necessity of regional ties.

Therefore, in Masoumi-Zare's view, any form of government established in the Iranian homeland must pursue security before all else from beyond the borders.

entry.title: [fazelimohammadir] God, keep us away from that patriotism that only shows up on days of victory.…
entry.summary:
Machine-translated from the original Telegram post.

Source: @fazelimohammadir

God, keep us away from that patriotism that only shows up on days of victory. Teach us to love Iran not when it aligns with our wishes, but precisely at the moment when we are angry with it, complaining about its rulers, and seeing its future as dark. God, protect us from the temptation of those saviors who must first set the land ablaze in order to build their promised tomorrow on its ashes. Do not let us be among those who sacrifice independence for the sake of freedom; the people for the sake of power; and Iran for the sake of proving their own righteousness. How easy it is to stand at a distance and prescribe courage for a people who must pay the price. How easy it is to want war when someone else's child must die in it. How easy it is to call destruction a "transition" when the house that is collapsing is not our house. God, save us from addiction to hatred; from that hatred that no longer wants truth, does not want a solution, and does not even want victory; it only wants the other to be destroyed, even if in the process, the homeland too is wounded. Give us the maturity to distinguish between opposition and revenge, between protest and destruction, between hope and illusion, and between saving a nation and seizing its future. God, do not let us one day become so thirsty for power that we shake the hand of any foreigner who promises tomorrow. Do not let us turn foreign policy from a strategy for Iran's interests into a tool for factional strife; today in the name of this group and tomorrow in the name of that group, but always at the expense of the country that must remain above us all. Do not let us put national security on the table of personal interest; for a contract, for wealth, for a position, for a share of power, or to guarantee our own future, let us not make the future of a people pay the price—a people who have no share in our bargain. Do not let us become so disgusted with today that we imagine any tomorrow as liberation, simply because it is different. Do not let us invoke the name of the people but in private think only of our own position after the storm. If we speak, let it not be for a share in tomorrow's power. If we oppose, let it not be to negotiate with potential victors. If we stand, let it not be in the ranks of this camp or that camp, but alongside a people who are always the first victims of the game of power. God, teach us that sometimes patriotism is not a shout, not a flag, not a slogan, but the ability to say a single "no": no to tyranny, no to disintegration, no to war, no to dependency, no to revenge, and no to a future that must be built by destroying Iran today.

Gradual Change or Revolution: The Importance of Parties in Iranian Society

Mohammadreza Jalaeipour, a sociology graduate and the head of the central council and head of the think tank of the Ahd-e Iran Party, in this conversation emphasizes the necessity of gradual change of the system based on three principles: justice, solidarity, and democracy. Drawing on new social theories, the experience of Middle Eastern countries, and global relations, he believes that to reach the ideals of society and development, institutional changes are needed — something that does not happen through revolutionary change.

Watch the conversation
https://youtu.be/LbqNo2jJNss

Jalaeipour argues that the reformists, despite their achievements over these years, have always defined themselves in opposition to a part of society, which has made a form of solidarity impossible.

Note: This interview was recorded before 18 and 19 Dey 1404 and before the US war against Iran, on 15 Dey 1404.
